subtype: Restless at work and searching for stimulation [Actor]
passage: Payal, you say the new job is "fine" but you spend half the day tidying your inbox? Let me tell you about me at twenty-five. I'm your Vandana Mausi, and back then I was a clerk at the district registrar's office. I finished my files by eleven. After that I sharpened pencils, restacked forms, walked to the window, came back. I felt guilty all afternoon, as if I were stealing my salary. I thought I was lazy. It took me a year to see it wasn't one thing. Some days I needed harder work, so I asked to help with the old land records nobody wanted. Some days I needed a reason, so I started helping elderly farmers fill forms at the counter. And some days, honestly, I was just tired and needed a proper lunch break, not a fourth cup of tea. So ask what your restlessness is asking for.

qa.q: By what time did Vandana finish her files at the registrar's office?
qa.a: She finished her files by eleven.

qa.q: Why did young Vandana feel guilty all afternoon?
qa.a: With nothing real to do, she felt she was stealing her salary, so the small distractions seemed like a personal failing rather than a sign the work didn't stretch her.

qa.q: What choices helped Vandana once she saw that her boredom had different causes?
qa.a: She asked for the harder land-records work, helped farmers with forms for a sense of purpose, and took a proper lunch break on days she was simply tired.

qa.q: How might Payal look at the inbox-tidying after this story?
qa.a: Payal might stop calling it laziness and ask whether the job needs more challenge, more purpose, or more rest.

grounding: An elder recalls being under-challenged at work, filling the day with small distractions and guilt, and learning to answer boredom with difficulty, meaning or rest.

subtype: Restless at work and searching for stimulation [Actor]
passage: For six weeks Gautam's team at the insurance office had been frozen by a merger. No new projects could start until the two companies agreed on software, and nobody knew when that would be. Gautam, twenty-five, answered two emails before ten and then drifted: news, a crossword, reorganising the stationery drawer, three trips to the vending machine. By evening he felt oddly guilty and exhausted, though he'd done almost nothing. His colleague Nikita found him labelling folders that didn't need labels. "Same," she said. "I've started learning the new claims rules from the manual, just to have something hard to chew on." Gautam thought about it. The next morning he asked his manager if he could draft training notes for when the merger went through. The afternoon flew.

qa.q: What had frozen Gautam's team for six weeks?
qa.a: A merger had frozen the team.

qa.q: Why did Gautam feel guilty and exhausted though he'd done almost nothing?
qa.a: Drifting through small distractions left him feeling useless, and the emptiness was tiring in itself; it felt like his fault even though the freeze wasn't.

qa.q: What choice did Gautam make, and why did it help?
qa.a: He asked to draft training notes for after the merger, which gave him both difficulty and a purpose, so the afternoon flew.

qa.q: What does Nikita's 'Same' do for Gautam?
qa.a: It tells Gautam he isn't alone in the drifting, and Nikita's example of chewing on the claims manual hints that something harder might help him too.

grounding: An under-challenged adult stuck in a work freeze fills the day with distractions and guilt, then finds relief in harder, meaningful work.

subtype: Lost in a game or puzzle [Actor]
passage: Saturday hobby club at the community library ended at one, but at twenty past, Trisha, ten, was still on the floor of the activity room with the gear kit. She was building a windmill whose blades turned when you wound a handle. On the first two tries, the gears slipped. On the third she moved the small gear one peg lower, held her breath and wound. The blades spun. She whooped, then immediately started on a second set of blades. Deepika Ma'am, the volunteer, was stacking chairs. "Trisha, your Papa's outside. And you haven't eaten your tiffin." Trisha looked up, blinking, as if waking. "It's already over?" The tiffin box sat unopened beside her, next to a heap of spare gears.

qa.q: What was Trisha building with the gear kit?
qa.a: A windmill whose blades turned when you wound a handle.

qa.q: What does Trisha's 'It's already over?' suggest about how she felt while building?
qa.a: She was so absorbed that time and hunger vanished 😊; the task was just hard enough to hold all her attention, and that felt joyful.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Trisha's building, and what did she do next?
qa.a: Moving the small gear one peg lower on the third try made the blades spin; instead of stopping, she began a second set, pulled on by a challenge that matched her skill.

qa.q: How might the scene look to Deepika Ma'am, stacking chairs?
qa.a: Deepika Ma'am sees a child so absorbed she missed the end of club and her lunch, and is probably amused and pleased while gently bringing her back to Papa waiting outside.

subtype: Lost in a game or puzzle [Actor]
passage: I'm Lakshmi, Sangeeta's older sister. On Sunday morning she tipped out the tub of building bricks and decided to build a bridge between the two beds, long enough for her toy bus to cross. It kept sagging in the middle. She frowned, pulled pieces off, tried a double layer, tried a pillar of stacked bricks underneath. I called her for breakfast twice. Nothing. Amma put a plate of idlis beside her, and she ate one without looking, still clicking bricks with her other hand. I don't know exactly what was going on in her head, but her tongue was poking out and she was humming. At half past twelve the bus rolled across. She sat back, beaming, and said, "Now a tunnel."

qa.q: What did Sangeeta want the bridge to carry?
qa.a: Her toy bus.

qa.q: What do Sangeeta's humming and poking tongue suggest about her state?

qa.q: What choice did Amma make, and why did it work well?
qa.a: Amma put the idlis beside Sangeeta instead of pulling her away, so she could eat without breaking her concentration on the bridge.

qa.q: How might being ignored at breakfast feel for Lakshmi?
qa.a: Lakshmi might be a little annoyed after calling twice for nothing, but also amused and impressed to see Sangeeta so wrapped up in the bridge 😄

grounding: An older sister watches a child so absorbed in a building-brick bridge that she forgets breakfast and the time.

passage: Siddiq arrived at the club nets in Durban still angry about a history mark, his phone buzzing with the group chat arguing about it. His friend Thabo was already padded up. "Bowl at me. That new leg-spin grip." The grip was just beyond him. The first balls floated wide. Then one turned, just a little. Siddiq focused on his wrist, the seam, a spot on the pitch. He tried again, and again, adjusting by millimetres. Thabo started playing and missing. Neither of them spoke much. When the floodlights came on, Siddiq realised his phone had been in the kit bag for two hours and he hadn't once thought of it, or of the history mark. Walking home, his head felt clear and quiet, like a swept room.

qa.q: Where had Siddiq's phone been for two hours?
qa.a: In the kit bag.

qa.q: How did Siddiq feel walking home, and why?
qa.a: Calm and clear, his head 'like a swept room'; two hours of full focus on a grip just beyond him had crowded out both the phone and the anger.

qa.a: Thabo asked for the new leg-spin grip, a task hard enough to need all of Siddiq's attention but close enough that one ball turned and kept him trying.

qa.a: Thabo got real practice against a turning ball and a friend who slowly calmed down; playing and missing was probably challenging in a good way.

grounding: A teenager practising a slightly-too-hard bowling grip forgets his phone and his anger and walks home calm and clear.

passage: The school music room was the only quiet place at lunch, and Parul, fifteen, had gone there every day that week. The music teacher had given her a new strumming pattern with a tricky off-beat, harder than anything she'd played but not impossible. On Thursday she sat on the low bench and began. Wrong. Slower. Nearly. Again. Her classmate Harish came in to fetch the tabla, called her name, and got no answer. The bell rang for fifth period. Parul jumped, looked at the clock and laughed. She hadn't checked her phone once; it was still in her locker. In chemistry she felt strangely calm, as if the forty minutes had cleared something out.

qa.q: Where did Parul practise during lunch?
qa.a: In the school music room.

qa.q: Why did Parul laugh when the bell rang?
qa.a: She was surprised at how the time had vanished 😄; she'd been so absorbed that the bell broke in like being woken up.

qa.q: Why did this pattern hold Parul's attention, and what could the teacher offer next?
qa.a: It was harder than anything she'd played but not impossible; once it becomes easy, the teacher could give a slightly harder pattern to keep her in that zone.

qa.q: How might Harish have seen Parul when she didn't answer?
qa.a: Harish might have felt puzzled or ignored at first, then realised Parul was completely lost in the practice.

grounding: A teenager practising a just-hard-enough guitar pattern forgets her phone and feels calm afterwards.

passage: Tarun, you say you only do good work "when the mood strikes"? Let me tell you about me at twenty-five, a young man in my father's carpentry workshop in Saharanpur. I'm Anand; my father called me the dreamer back then. Some days I carved beautifully and lost whole afternoons in the wood. Most days customers wandered in, my cousin chattered, and I did bits of ten jobs. My father said, "Good days don't fall from the sky. You make room for them." So each morning I chose one piece and chalked on the wall what "done" would look like. I put up a sign: "Orders after four." And I always chose a pattern a little harder than my last one. Those lost-in-the-wood afternoons started coming three, four times a week.

qa.q: What sign did Anand put up in the workshop?
qa.a: 'Orders after four.'

qa.q: How did young Anand feel on the afternoons he carved well?
qa.a: Anand felt absorbed and happy, so lost in the wood that whole afternoons slipped by, unlike the scattered days of bits of ten jobs.

qa.q: What three changes did Anand make, and why did they work?
qa.a: He chose one piece with a clear 'done', kept customers until after four, and picked a pattern a little harder than his last; together these built the conditions for absorbed work.

qa.q: What might Tarun change after hearing this?
qa.a: Tarun might stop waiting for the mood and try setting one clear goal and blocking interruptions for the work that matters most.

grounding: An elder recalls building the conditions for absorbed work: clear goals, fewer interruptions and tasks just above his skill.

passage: The flat next door was being renovated, drills from nine to five, and Asif's roommate Karthik worked from the same small living room, on calls half the day. Asif, a data analyst, had been trying to finish a forecasting model for three weeks and kept getting nowhere. On Sunday he made a plan. He wrote Monday's single goal on a card: finish the cleaning step for the sales data. He moved his desk to the balcony, bought cheap foam earplugs, and turned off chat alerts until noon. He also chose to try the new method his manager had shown him, just past what he was sure of. On Monday, drills and all, he looked up at 12:10 and found the step done and his tea cold. Karthik waved through the glass, grinning.

qa.q: What did Asif write on the card?
qa.a: Finish the cleaning step for the sales data.

qa.q: What might Asif have felt when he looked up at 12:10?
qa.a: Surprise and quiet satisfaction 🙂; the cold tea shows he'd been absorbed for hours despite the drills.

qa.q: Which of Asif's choices built the conditions for focus, and why?
qa.a: One clear goal, a quieter spot with earplugs and alerts off, and a method just past his comfort; together they cut interruptions and gave him a task worth sinking into.

qa.q: How might Karthik be affected by Asif's move to the balcony?
qa.a: Karthik gets the living room for calls without worrying about disturbing Asif, and seems glad, waving and grinning through the glass.

grounding: An adult in a noisy flat sets one clear goal, cuts interruptions and picks a slightly harder method, and gets absorbed in the work.

passage:
"Manoj, nets tomorrow? I'll bowl with you."
"Whatever, bhaiya."
Siddharth lowered his phone. "Whatever? You used to beg me."
"What's the point?" Manoj kept his eyes on the TV. "Every time I bowl, Coach says no-ball. I tried a shorter run-up. No-ball. I tried starting further back. No-ball. He shouts, and the whole team laughs."
"So you've stopped?"
"I'm just bad. Doesn't matter what I do."
Siddharth came and sat beside him. "Last Sunday you bowled four good ones to me in the lane."
"That's the lane. That's different."
"Maybe. Or maybe we mark your stride with chalk and sort out the no-ball together. Just ten balls."
Manoj shrugged. "You'll see. Same thing will happen."
But he didn't say no.

qa.q: What does Coach keep saying when Manoj bowls?
qa.a: Coach says no-ball.

qa.q: Why does 'Whatever' feel like the sensible answer to Manoj?
qa.a: He changed his run-up twice and still got no-ball and laughter; when effort seems to change nothing, not trying at least spares him more shame.

qa.q: What choice does Siddharth make, and why might it help?
qa.a: Instead of arguing, he recalls the four good balls and offers a small shared fix, chalk marks and just ten balls, a chance for effort to visibly work.

qa.q: How does Siddharth seem to feel hearing 'Whatever'?
qa.a: Siddharth seems surprised and concerned, since Manoj used to beg to play, and cares enough to put down his phone and sit beside him.

grounding: A child whose bowling keeps getting called and laughed at, whatever he changes, stops trying and says whatever.

passage: When I was nine, my Hemant Mama checked my maths homework every night after his shop closed. I'm Raghav. Every mistake got a sharp tap on the page and "Careless again!" I tried going slower. Still careless. I tried checking twice. Still wrong somewhere, still "careless". After a few months I stopped trying to get them right. I'd write any number and wait for the tap. When Amma asked why I'd gone so quiet, I said, "Whatever I do, it's wrong." It felt true. I'm eleven now, and Amma found me a tuition teacher who marks what I got right first. Last week I got four out of six, and I actually wanted to know what went wrong in the other two. That felt strange.

qa.q: What did Hemant Mama say at every mistake?
qa.a: 'Careless again!'

qa.q: Why did writing any number feel reasonable to Raghav at nine?
qa.a: Going slower and checking twice still brought the same tap and 'careless', so effort seemed useless and guessing at least cost less.

qa.q: What changed for Raghav, and why did it help?
qa.a: A tuition teacher who marks what Raghav got right first; seeing four out of six correct showed that effort counts, so Raghav wanted to fix the rest.

qa.q: What might Amma have noticed that led her to find a new teacher?
qa.a: Amma saw Raghav go quiet and heard 'Whatever I do, it's wrong', and seems to have understood the problem was the constant criticism, not laziness.

grounding: A child criticised for every mistake whatever the effort stops trying, until a different teacher shows that effort counts.

subtype: Not asking for help at home [Actor]
passage:
Tuesday
Yogesh Chacha asked at dinner what I want for my birthday. Everyone looked at me. I said, "Anything is fine." He said, "No, really, Swati. What would make you happy?" I said it again. Anything.
The truth is I want a sketchbook, the thick one with cream pages. But in the old house nobody ever heard what I wanted. Five cousins, one room, everybody tired. I stopped asking around Class 6. It just seemed smarter.
Chachi said, "You can tell us later if you think of something." She said it so gently.
Here it's different. Nobody laughs. They ask twice. I know that. So why does my mouth still say "anything"?
Maybe tomorrow I'll write "sketchbook" on a chit and leave it on the fridge.

qa.q: What does Swati actually want for the birthday?
qa.a: A sketchbook, the thick one with cream pages.

qa.q: Why does Swati still say 'anything' even though things have changed?
qa.a: Swati still feels wary of asking: years of wishes going unheard in the old house taught Swati that asking was pointless, and that belief speaks first even with people who ask twice.

qa.q: What small step does Swati consider, and why might it be a good start?
qa.a: Writing 'sketchbook' on a chit for the fridge; it is a low-risk way to voice a wish and find out that here it is heard.

qa.q: How might Yogesh Chacha feel hearing 'Anything is fine' twice?
qa.a: He may feel a little sad and puzzled, wanting to make Swati happy, and aware it will take patience for Swati to trust that wishes matter now.

grounding: A teenager whose wishes went unheard in a crowded home no longer voices them, even in a new home that listens.

passage: It's small, the thing I'm proudest of this year. I'm Reena, I teach anatomy at a nursing college in Kozhikode, and in the first term I had a student called Yusuf. Clever, quick, the best questions in week one. By week four he'd look at a test paper and write "I can't do this" across the top before reading a single question. His first mark had been poor, and he'd decided that was who he was. So I stopped handing him full tests. I gave him one diagram of the hand bones, just ten labels. He got nine. The next week, a diagram of the foot. Then one short answer. By March he sat the whole paper. He didn't top it. But he didn't write "can't" either.

qa.q: What did Reena give Yusuf instead of a full test?
qa.a: One diagram of the hand bones, just ten labels.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf write 'I can't do this' before reading a question?
qa.a: After one poor mark he decided failing was who he was, so trying seemed pointless and giving up first protected him from another disappointment.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it work?
qa.a: Getting nine of ten labels on a small diagram; small successes, built up week by week, gave Yusuf evidence that his effort did count.

qa.q: What was it like for Reena to watch a capable student give up?
qa.a: Reena clearly noticed the gap between his sharp early questions and the 'can't', and seems more determined than annoyed, choosing small tasks over lectures.

grounding: A teacher sees a capable student declare defeat before starting and gives small tasks he can succeed at, slowly changing his belief.

passage: I'm Payal, and I teach accounts at an evening college in Nagpur. Vandana, nineteen, works in a pharmacy by day and comes to my class at six. In the first week she solved a ledger problem faster than anyone. After she failed the first unit test, something shut. Now when I hand out problems, she pushes the sheet an inch away and says, "Ma'am, I'm not an accounts person. No use." I can't know everything she's carrying. But last Tuesday I skipped the worksheet for her and gave her just one entry: record a cash sale of five hundred rupees. She hesitated, wrote it, and looked up. "That's it?" "That's it. Correct." On Thursday I gave her three. Today she asked for the worksheet herself.

qa.a: Record a cash sale of five hundred rupees.

qa.q: What does Vandana's 'That's it?' suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Surprise and a flicker of relief; after expecting to fail, getting one task right challenged her belief that effort was no use.

qa.a: She gave Vandana one small entry, then three; small wins built evidence that trying works, until Vandana asked for the worksheet herself.

qa.a: Vandana may feel that Payal hasn't given up on her and isn't forcing her either, which makes it safer to try again.

grounding: A teacher sees a capable student give up before starting and gives one small task she can do, then a few more.

subtype: Stuck in an unresponsive job or home [Actor]
passage: Looking back at last year, I think I just went quiet inside. I'm Dolma, and I was working at a travel agency in Gangtok. I asked my manager for a proper chair for my back, then for a fixed day off, then for training on the booking software. Each time: a nod, then nothing. By autumn I'd stopped asking. I'd sit, do the tickets, go home, and feel nothing much, not even angry. My friend Anirban noticed I'd stopped laughing at his terrible jokes. He asked, "When did you last want something?" I couldn't answer, and that scared me. He sat with me while I booked a session with the counsellor at the district health centre. Talking there helped me see the numbness had a reason. I'm in a new job now, still learning to ask again.

qa.q: What three things did Dolma ask the manager for?
qa.a: A proper chair, a fixed day off, and training on the booking software.

qa.q: Why did Dolma stop asking by autumn?
qa.a: Every request met a nod and then nothing, so asking seemed useless; going quiet felt safer than being ignored again, even though it left Dolma numb.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what step followed?
qa.a: Anirban's question, 'When did you last want something?', which Dolma couldn't answer; Anirban then sat with Dolma while a session with a counsellor was booked.

qa.a: Anirban noticed Dolma had stopped laughing at his jokes, a sign the numbness was spreading beyond work, so he cared enough to ask and to stay while the session was booked.

subtype: Stuck in an unresponsive job or home [Actor]
passage:
Supervisor's note, hospital records department, Thrissur. Mercy, 14 November.
Joseph has worked here two years. In his first year he sent me requests often: a second monitor, a change in the night rota, a place on the coding course. Most went up the line and never came back. Partly my fault; I stopped chasing them. This month I noticed he no longer asks for anything. He finishes his files, eats alone and says "fine" to every question in the same flat voice. Today I sat with him and apologised for the unanswered requests. I've pushed the coding course through myself; he starts in January. I also told him, gently, that if the heaviness stays or feels like too much, talking with a counsellor could really help, and gave him the details of the staff counselling service. He nodded, and for the first time in weeks he looked up.

qa.q: When does Joseph start the coding course?
qa.a: He starts in January.

qa.q: What does Joseph's flat 'fine' suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests numbness; after so many requests vanished, caring seemed pointless, so he stopped wanting things out loud.

qa.q: What choices did Mercy make, and why do they matter?
qa.a: Mercy apologised, pushed the coding course through, and gently pointed him to the staff counselling service; a real response shows asking can work, and the counsellor is there if the heaviness stays.

qa.q: What might Mercy be feeling as she writes this note?
qa.a: Mercy seems regretful about her part in the silence and determined to set it right, and relieved to see Joseph look up.

grounding: A supervisor notices an adult whose requests were ignored has stopped asking and seems numb, and responds and suggests a counsellor.

passage: Ujjwal's kite had torn on the neem tree, and there was no money for a new one before Sankranti. His grandfather, Kishore Dada, handed him a bowl of flour paste, old newspaper and thread. "Your kite. You decide how to fix it." The sun was already low. Ujjwal patched the hole with a big square of newspaper. On the roof the kite dipped and crashed. Too heavy on one side, he thought. He peeled half the patch off, cut a smaller one, and stuck a scrap on the other side to balance it. Dada said nothing, just held the spool. On the second try the kite wobbled, then climbed, steady, just before dark. Ujjwal stared up at it. "I did that," he whispered. "The patch did that."

qa.q: What did Kishore Dada hand Ujjwal?
qa.a: A bowl of flour paste, old newspaper and thread.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's whisper 'I did that' show about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels proud and a bit amazed, seeing that his own decision about the patch is what made the kite fly.

qa.q: What choice by Kishore Dada helped Ujjwal learn that his actions matter?
qa.a: He let Ujjwal decide the repair and stayed quiet even after the crash, so the success clearly came from Ujjwal's own fix.

qa.q: What might Kishore Dada feel watching the kite climb?
qa.a: Probably quiet pride and pleasure, glad he held back his advice so Ujjwal could discover the fix himself.

passage: In the Chennai flats, Farhan Uncle from the fourth floor gave Ganga, eight, an old plastic bottle made into a bird feeder. "Your job. You choose where it goes." Ganga hung it by the balcony door, where she could see it from her bed. For three days, no birds. Just ants. She sat on the step and thought. The pigeons liked the parapet; she'd seen them. The spot by the door was dark and next to the washing. So she moved the feeder to the sunny corner by the parapet and swept away the ants. On Saturday morning she shouted so loudly that Farhan Uncle looked up from the courtyard: two sparrows, pecking. "I moved it," she told him proudly. "That's why."

qa.q: Where did Ganga first hang the feeder?
qa.a: By the balcony door, where she could see it from her bed.

qa.q: What was Ganga thinking as she sat on the step after three days?
qa.a: She was puzzling out why no birds came, remembering the pigeons on the parapet and noticing that the first spot was dark and next to the washing.

qa.q: Which choice made the difference, and what did Ganga learn from it?
qa.a: Moving the feeder to the sunny corner by the parapet; when the sparrows came, she saw that her own decision had caused it.

qa.q: How might Farhan Uncle feel hearing 'I moved it. That's why'?
qa.a: Farhan Uncle would probably be delighted that giving Ganga the choice paid off, and see how proud she is of working it out herself 😊

grounding: A child chooses where to hang a bird feeder, moves it after it fails, and sees birds come because of her decision.

passage: Pranav, you asked how I kept going this winter, with Papa in hospital for so long and Mumma at his bedside every evening. Honestly, at first I just lay on my bed feeling like everything was happening to us and I couldn't do a thing. Then I told Mrs Menon, the school counsellor, that I couldn't concentrate. She listened, said it made sense to feel that way, and asked me to draw a line down a page. Left side: things I can't control. Papa's recovery, the hospital bills, Mumma being tired. Right side: things I can. My two hours of study after school. Making dal so Mumma eats something hot. Calling Nani when I feel scared. Telling Mrs Menon each Friday how I'm doing. I still cry sometimes. But I have a right side now. I'm Ishita, and that page is still in my bag.

qa.q: What did Mrs Menon ask Ishita to draw?
qa.a: A line down a page.

qa.q: Why did Ishita feel unable to do a thing at first?
qa.a: Ishita felt helpless and scared: with Papa in hospital and Mumma away every evening, events seemed to be happening to the family, and Ishita couldn't change the big things.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Ishita do after it?
qa.a: Telling Mrs Menon, who listened and helped make the two-sided list; Ishita then acted on the right side: study hours, making dal, calling Nani and Friday check-ins.

qa.q: How might Mumma experience Ishita making the dal?
qa.a: Coming home tired from the hospital, Mumma finds something hot to eat and sees Ishita coping, which may ease a little of her worry.

grounding: A teenager facing a parent's long illness lists what is and isn't in their control with a counsellor's help and acts on the first list.

passage: I'm Ritu, Kalyani's cousin, and I stayed with her family for a month during my internship. Her parents had just told her they were separating, and the house was full of low, tense conversations. Kalyani stopped eating dinner with us and spent evenings staring at her ceiling. One night she said to me, "It's all decided. Nothing I do matters." I sat on her bed and said it made sense to feel that way, and that none of it was her fault. Then I handed her a notebook. "Two columns. What you can't change, and what you can." She wrote slowly. Can't: where Papa will live. Can: badminton practice, board prep, talking to Masi, seeing the school counsellor. By the end of the week she was back at badminton, and she'd booked a talk with the counsellor herself.

qa.q: What did Ritu hand Kalyani?
qa.a: A notebook.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she said 'Nothing I do matters'?
qa.a: Helpless and alone; the separation was decided without her, so it seemed nothing she did could make any difference.

qa.q: What choice did Ritu make that night, and why did it help?
qa.a: Ritu stayed, told Kalyani it wasn't her fault, and helped her split things into can and can't; acting on the 'can' column gave Kalyani back some control.

qa.q: How might Kalyani's parents see her return to badminton?
qa.a: They would probably feel some relief, seeing their daughter finding her feet during a painful time for the whole family.

grounding: A cousin helps a teenager facing her parents' separation list what she can and cannot control, and acting on the first restores some power.
